name: communication
description: Taking action to share information with another.
perceptions: I want to let another know something.
It may be a specific piece of information or an indirect signal.

guidance.description: Effective communication is an essential skill for achieving success in all areas of life, whether personal or professional. The challenge of how to be an effective communicator gets far easier when you follow these seven steps.

variations.name: win-lose negotiation
variations.description: Trying to reach a more positive outcome for yourself by engaging in a back-and-forth sharing of proposals with another.
perceptions: I need to come to an agreement with someone.
This is a win-lose situation where there's a limited resource.
I need to get as much of it as I can.

guidance.description: Negotiation can be unpredictable. Regardless of how much preparation and research you do, you can’t control how your counterpart responds. For this reason, you may struggle to manage your emotions during negotiation or avoid it altogether. Yet, you can improve your chances of negotiating successfully. How you approach it and the tactics you use are essential to achieving your desired outcomes.

variations.name: win-win negotiation
variations.description: Trying to reach a more positive outcome for all sides by engaging in a back-and-forth sharing of proposals with another.
perceptions: I need to come to an agreement with someone.
This may be a win-win situation where everyone can benefit.

guidance.description: The success of a business deal typically depends on offering fair contractual terms to the negotiating parties. A win-win negotiating strategy involves considering every party's interests and drafting a business deal that meets their needs and yours.

variations.name: small talk
variations.description: Engaging in communication where the content is not nearly as relevant as the act of communicating.
perceptions: I'm here with this person for a time.
I want them to know that I'm friendly.
They might be someone interesting.
It sends a message if I won't talk with them.
desires: desire to be perceived a certain way
examples: Meeting a new person at a party.
Being stuck with someone on a broken elevator.
Running into a neighbor at the store.

guidance.description: 7 Ways to Be Amazing at Small Talk

variations.name: first party socializing
variations.description: Talking with someone to better understand them and to further the relationship. This can be with an old friend or someone you've never met.
perceptions: It could be interesting, enjoyable, and useful to talk with this person or group.

guidance.description: We all have awkward moments when we wish we could be more social—whether we're introverts or not. Social skills can be developed without changing who you are.

comparisons.description: 'Small talk' is what you do to fill social time when you want to send a message that you're sociable, but don't want to get deep right now. You can make small talk with strangers or close friends. 'First party socializing' is when the content gets more relevant and the relationships deepen. 'Third party socializing' is when you talk about people who aren't present. Hopefully, this happens mostly with friends and neighbors.

variations.name: third party socializing
variations.description: Participating in social knowledge transfer about someone not present to further a different relationship.
perceptions: I can bond with this person or group by talking with them.
Talking about someone else is always an interesting topic.

guidance.description: Gossip, whether we like to admit it or not, is a common thread woven into the fabric of our social lives. It serves various social functions and has both advantages and disadvantages, depending on how it's used.

variations.name: bragging
variations.description: A perception that someone is trying to impress someone else by unnecessarily boosting themselves or downplaying others.
perceptions: That person is highlighting something positive about themself or downplaying someone else.
They're trying to score social points.
Hard to tell how much they may be exaggerating.
examples: Don't watch me flex if you don't like big guns.
At least my hair is naturally curly.

guidance.description: If you want to learn the best approaches to handle braggers in a positive and assertive manner, read on.

variations.name: clear communication
variations.description: A perception that someone's communication expresses the intended point in an efficient way.
perceptions: That person has said or done something that lets me understand something important.
Because of this information, I can consider what's next.
results: The contents of the communication may be perceived as positive, neutral, or negative.
examples: The great professor made a complex subject enjoyable.
My enemy made it very clear that I'm next.

variations.name: confusing communication
variations.description: A perception that someone's communication does not help us understand what's intended.
perceptions: That person has said or done something that does not help me understand.
Because I don't know what they're trying to say, I can't act on this information.
results: The contents of the communication may be unknown, uncertain, hopeful, or worrying.
examples: The poor professor made a complex subject impenetrable.
My enemy made a confusing threat.

commentaries.quote: Communication—the human connection—is the key to personal and career success.
The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place.
So much of life is a negotiation – so even if you're not in business, you have opportunities to practice all around you.
He who has learned to disagree without being disagreeable has discovered the most valuable secret of a diplomat.
Sharing impressive things about yourself may seem like a shortcut to social credit, but it will backfire if you can't take an interest in others.
